meta.title: How RAG Works: Grounding LLMs in Your Own Data
meta.thesis: RAG fixes the biggest weakness of language models — confidently making things up — by retrieving real passages from your own documents and answering from them.

modules.title: Why RAG exists
modules.sub: Start here — the problem before the machinery.
modules.summary: A language model only knows what it saw in training. Ask it about your internal docs and it will often answer fluently and wrongly. RAG exists to ground answers in retrieved, real text.
modules.decisionItForces: Should this question be answered from the model's memory, or from retrieved documents?
objectives: Recognize when RAG is the right tool

blocks.title: The confidently-wrong problem
blocks.analogy: An ungrounded LLM is like a smart intern who never says 'I don't know' — they'll answer your billing question with total confidence, inventing the policy.

spans.text: A language model predicts likely text. Ask it something outside its training and it still produces a fluent answer — that is a
fixes this by fetching real passages from your documents and instructing the model to answer only from them.
Before reading on, predict: if your help-center changes a refund window from 14 to 30 days, why might a plain (non-RAG) chatbot still say 14?

blocks.title: Support desk, with and without grounding

spans.text: A customer asks: 'Can I return a sale item?'

items.text: the model guesses from generic e-commerce norms — sometimes right, sometimes inventing your policy.
it retrieves your actual 'Sale & clearance returns' article and answers from that exact wording, with a citation.

spans.text: How this breaks: RAG is only as fresh as its index. If you forget to re-index after a policy change, retrieval returns the OLD passage and the model grounds confidently in stale truth. Re-indexing on publish is part of the system, not an afterthought.

modules.title: The RAG pipeline
modules.sub: Now the moving parts that turn docs into grounded answers.
modules.summary: RAG is a pipeline: ingest documents, split them into chunks, embed each chunk into a vector, store the vectors, then at query time retrieve the closest chunks and generate an answer from them.
objectives: Name the five stages of a RAG pipeline

blocks.title: Click through the pipeline
blocks.caption: Each stage's output is the next stage's input.

steps.label: Ingest
steps.detail: Load source documents (help articles, PDFs, tickets) into a normalized text form.

steps.label: Chunk
steps.detail: Split each document into passages small enough to embed and retrieve precisely — often 200–500 tokens with slight overlap.

steps.label: Embed
steps.detail: Convert each chunk into a vector that captures its meaning, so similar passages sit close together.

steps.label: Store
steps.detail: Write vectors (plus the original text + metadata) into a vector database with an index for fast nearest-neighbor search.

steps.label: Retrieve
steps.detail: Embed the user's question, find the top-k closest chunks.

steps.label: Generate
steps.detail: Put the retrieved chunks in the prompt and ask the model to answer ONLY from them, with citations.

modules.title: Chunking & embeddings
modules.sub: The indexing half — make meaning searchable.
modules.summary: Retrieval quality is mostly decided here. Chunk too big and you retrieve noise; too small and you lose context. Embeddings place chunks in a space where 'near' means 'similar in meaning'.
objectives: Read code that builds an index

blocks.title: Meaning as coordinates
blocks.analogy: An embedding is like placing every passage on a map where related ideas are neighbors — 'refund' sits near 'return', far from 'shipping speed'.

spans.text: is a list of numbers positioning a chunk by meaning.
then ranks chunks by distance to the question's embedding, so it matches on meaning, not just keywords.

blocks.title: Nearest in meaning
blocks.caption: Pick a query — its three nearest passages light up. Notice meaning, not exact words, drives closeness.

blocks.title: Build the index
blocks.code:
from my_rag import load_docs, chunk, embed, VectorStore

docs = load_docs("help_center/")
chunks = chunk(docs, size=400, overlap=50)

store = VectorStore(dim=1536)
for c in chunks:
    store.add(vector=embed(c.text), text=c.text, meta=c.meta)

store.save("help.index")

predictThenReveal.prompt: What breaks if you set size=4000 with no overlap?
predictThenReveal.answer: Chunks get huge: each retrieved passage carries lots of irrelevant text (lower precision), and a fact split across a boundary can be missed entirely because there is no overlap to capture it.

syntax.explains: Splits documents into ~400-token passages, repeating 50 tokens between neighbors so facts on a boundary aren't lost.
Turns a chunk's text into its meaning-vector.
Saves the vector alongside the original text and metadata so retrieval can return readable, citable passages.

modules.title: Retrieve & generate
modules.sub: The query half — answer from what you found.
modules.summary: At query time you embed the question, pull the top-k nearest chunks, and assemble a prompt that tells the model to answer only from those passages. Get this contract right and grounding holds.
modules.decisionItForces: How many chunks (k) to retrieve, and whether to re-rank them.
objectives: Choose a starting value for k
Decide when re-ranking is worth it

blocks.title: Retrieve, then answer
blocks.code:
store = VectorStore.load("help.index")

def answer(question):
    hits = store.search(embed(question), k=4)
    context = "\n---\n".join(h.text for h in hits)
    prompt = (
        "Answer ONLY from the context. If absent, say you don't know.\n\n"
        f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
    )
    return llm(prompt), [h.meta for h in hits]

predictThenReveal.prompt: A user asks something your docs don't cover. With this prompt, what should happen?
predictThenReveal.answer: Retrieval still returns the 4 closest chunks, but none contain the answer — so the instruction 'if absent, say you don't know' should make the model decline instead of inventing one. That refusal is the system working, not failing.

blocks.useWhen: Top-k retrieval already surfaces the right passage in the first few hits.
blocks.avoidWhen: The right chunk often ranks 8th–15th — then add a re-ranker to reorder a larger candidate set.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: Start simple: k=4, no re-ranking. Add re-ranking only when you measure recall problems.

options.text: Ground answers in retrieved, real passages
Replace the need for a language model

questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant passages and has the model answer from them, reducing hallucination.

options.text: So a fact split across a boundary isn't lost

questions.explanation: Overlap repeats a little text between neighboring chunks so boundary-spanning facts stay retrievable.

questions.prompt: Your index wasn't refreshed after a policy change. Most likely result?

options.text: It grounds confidently in the stale passage

questions.explanation: Retrieval returns the old chunk, so the answer is fluent and wrong — why re-indexing on publish matters.

questions.prompt: In one sentence, when would you reach for a re-ranker?
questions.acceptableAnswer: When the correct passage frequently exists in the candidate set but ranks too low for a small top-k, so re-ordering a larger candidate list surfaces it.
questions.explanation: Re-ranking helps recall when the right chunk is retrieved but not near the top.

rag.label: RAG
rag.laymanDefinition: A pattern where the system first retrieves relevant passages from your documents, then asks the model to answer using them.
rag.technicalNote: Decouples knowledge (the index) from reasoning (the model), so you update facts by re-indexing, not re-training.

hallucination.label: Hallucination
hallucination.laymanDefinition: When a model states something false with full confidence because it is predicting plausible text, not checking facts.

context-window.label: Context window
context-window.laymanDefinition: The maximum amount of text a model can consider at once — retrieved chunks plus the question plus the answer must fit inside it.

embedding.label: Embedding
embedding.laymanDefinition: A list of numbers that represents a piece of text by meaning, so similar texts have nearby vectors.
embedding.technicalNote: Typically produced by an embedding model; similarity is measured by cosine distance or dot product.

vector-db.label: Vector database
vector-db.laymanDefinition: A store built to save embeddings and find the nearest ones to a query vector quickly.
vector-db.technicalNote: Uses approximate nearest-neighbor indexes (e.g., HNSW) to keep search fast at scale.

chunking.label: Chunking
chunking.laymanDefinition: Splitting documents into smaller passages so retrieval can return precise, relevant pieces.

semantic-search.label: Semantic search
semantic-search.laymanDefinition: Searching by meaning rather than exact keywords, by comparing embedding vectors.

top-k.label: Top-k
top-k.laymanDefinition: The number of nearest passages you retrieve for a query — e.g., k=4 returns the four closest chunks.

reranking.label: Re-ranking
reranking.laymanDefinition: A second pass that reorders a larger set of retrieved candidates to push the most relevant ones to the top.
